pronunciation.title: Say it right from day one

rules.explain: a=AH, e=EH, i=EE, o=OH, u=OO. Always. So CASA is KAH-sah.

rules.rule: H is silent, J sounds like H
rules.explain: HOLA is OH-lah (no H sound). J in JUEVES sounds like English H: HWEH-vehs.
Ñ is like NY in canyon: NIÑO = NEEN-yoh. LL and Y sound like Y in yes.
Tap your tongue once for R. PERRO (dog) rolls longer than PERO (but).
Most words stress the middle: HOLA = OH-lah, GRACIAS = GRAH-syahs. An accent mark (á) forces stress there.

alphabet.title: The Spanish alphabet: 27 letters
alphabet.explain: Spanish uses the same letters as English plus Ñ. Letter names matter for spelling your name aloud. Read each name, then say the example word.

letters.tip: soft, like TH in this: DÍA
Y in yes, or EE alone: YO

counting.title: Counting 0 to 100
counting.explain: Learn 0–15 by heart. 16–19 = DIEZ + number stuck together (dieciséis). 20s = VEINTI + number (veintidós). 30+ = tens + Y + ones (treinta y uno). 100 = CIEN (cien alone, ciento + more).
rules: 30–99 use Y: treinta y uno (31), cuarenta y dos (42).
CIEN = exactly 100; CIENTO + more: ciento uno (101).

lessons.title: Hello! Greetings and politeness
lessons.learn: Start with the magic words. Say HOLA to anyone, anytime. Spanish greets the day in parts: morning (buenos días), afternoon/evening (buenas tardes), night (buenas noches). POR FAVOR (please) and GRACIAS (thanks) open every door.

grammar.title: Every noun is EL or LA
grammar.explain: Spanish nouns are masculine (EL) or feminine (LA). Words ending in -o are usually EL; words ending in -a are usually LA. Learn each noun WITH its el/la — never alone.
grammar.pattern: el + masculine noun · la + feminine noun
mistakes: Saying LA libro — libro is masculine: EL libro.
Forgetting el/la and saying just Casa — say LA casa.

lessons.title: Numbers and introductions
lessons.learn: Numbers 1–10 unlock prices, ages, and phone numbers. To introduce yourself use SER (to be): SOY = I am. Soy Ana = I am Ana. To ask a name: ¿CÓMO TE LLAMAS? (What are you called?).

grammar.title: SER: soy, eres, es (I am, you are, he/she is)
grammar.explain: SER describes who you are: name, origin, job. SOY = I am, ERES = you are, ES = he/she is. Drop the pronoun: SOY Ana is enough — no YO needed.
mistakes: Saying YO SOY Ana every time — SOY Ana is natural.
Using ES for yourself — I am is SOY, never ES.

lessons.title: ¿De dónde eres? Países, nacionalidades, idiomas
lessons.learn: Origin takes ser + de: SOY DE MÉXICO. Nationalities agree like adjectives (mexicano / mexicana) and are not capitalised. Languages: HABLO ESPAÑOL Y UN POCO DE INGLÉS.

grammar.title: Origin and nationality
grammar.pattern: soy de + country · soy + nationality · hablo + language
grammar.explain: Soy de México, pero vivo en Sevilla. Soy mexicana. Hablo español y un poco de inglés. «¿De dónde eres?» asks origin; «¿Dónde vives?» asks where you are now.

examples.t: Ella es de Argentina y vive en Madrid.
examples.r: EH-yah es deh ar-hen-TEE-nah ee BEE-veh en mah-DREED.
examples.en: She is from Argentina and lives in Madrid.

mistakes.why: Origin and nationality are different slots: de + place, bare adjective.
Most country names take no article after de.

dialogue.r: soy deh MEH-hee-koh, PEH-roh BEE-voh en mah-DREED.

lessons.title: Family and TENER (age)
lessons.learn: Meet the family: MADRE (mother), PADRE (father), HERMANO/A (brother/sister). Age uses TENER (to have), not 'to be': TENGO 10 AÑOS = I have 10 years = I am 10 years old.

grammar.title: TENER for age: tengo… años
grammar.explain: TENGO = I have, TIENES = you have, TIENE = he/she has. For age: TENGO + number + AÑOS. Ask age: ¿CUÁNTOS AÑOS TIENES? (How many years do you have?).
mistakes: Saying SOY diez años — age always uses TENER.
Saying AÑOS without T: ANOS is a rude word — say AHN-yohs with Ñ!

lessons.title: Food and -AR verbs
lessons.learn: Food first! AGUA, PAN, LECHE, MANZANA. To order, use QUIERO (I want) or QUISIERA (I would like, politer). Most Spanish verbs end in -AR: HABLAR (to speak) → HABLO (I speak), HABLAS (you speak), HABLA (he/she speaks).

grammar.title: Present -AR verbs: hablo, hablas, habla
grammar.explain: Take off -AR, add -O (I), -AS (you), -A (he/she). HABLAR → hablo, hablas, habla. This one pattern speaks hundreds of verbs: COMO (I eat), BEBO? No — BEBER is -ER. For now: -AR only!
mistakes: Saying YO HABLAS for 'I speak' — I = HABLO, you = HABLAS.

lessons.title: Mi casa: habitaciones, muebles y «hay»
lessons.learn: Rooms and furniture are described with HAY (there is / there are): EN MI CASA HAY DOS HABITACIONES. HAY never changes for number — one form serves both.

grammar.title: hay and possession
grammar.pattern: hay + noun · mi / tu / su + noun
grammar.explain: En el salón hay una mesa grande. Mi dormitorio es pequeño pero tiene mucha luz. hay states existence; tener states what a room has.

examples.t: En la cocina hay una mesa.
examples.r: en lah koh-SEE-nah eye OO-nah MEH-sah.
examples.en: In the kitchen there is a table.

mistakes.why: hay is invariable; no plural form.

mistakes.right: En mi casa hay tres habitaciones. / Mi casa tiene tres habitaciones.
mistakes.why: hay states existence in a place; tener states what something has.

dialogue.t: No es grande. En el salón hay una mesa y un sofá.
dialogue.r: noh es GRAHN-deh. en el sah-LOHN eye OO-nah MEH-sah ee oon soh-FAH.
dialogue.en: It isn't big. In the living room there is a table and a sofa.

dialogue.t: Dos: un dormitorio y un despacho pequeño.
dialogue.r: dohs: oon dor-mee-TOH-ree-oh ee oon des-PAH-choh peh-KEH-nyoh.
dialogue.en: Two: a bedroom and a small study.

lessons.title: Days, months, and telling time
lessons.learn: Days and months are lowercase in Spanish: LUNES, ENERO. Time: ES LA UNA (it is one) but SON LAS DOS (two). Ask: ¿QUÉ HORA ES? Answer: SON LAS + number.

grammar.title: Telling time: es la… / son las…
grammar.explain: ES LA UNA (1:00 — singular), SON LAS DOS/TRES… (plural). Half past: Y MEDIA — SON LAS TRES Y MEDIA (3:30). Quarter: Y CUARTO.
grammar.pattern: es la una · son las + number (+ y media)
mistakes: Saying SON LA UNA — one o'clock is ES LA UNA.
Capitalising days (Lunes) — Spanish days are lowercase.

lessons.title: El tiempo y las estaciones: hace frío, llueve
lessons.learn: Weather uses HACER for most states: HACE FRÍO, HACE SOL — and dedicated verbs for rain and snow: LLUEVE, NIEVA. Seasons take en: EN INVIERNO.

grammar.title: Weather with hacer
grammar.pattern: hace + frío/calor/sol/viento · llueve / nieva · en + season
grammar.explain: Hoy hace frío y llueve. En verano hace mucho calor, en invierno nieva en la sierra. «hace» is the third person of hacer and never takes a subject pronoun.

examples.t: En invierno nieva en la montaña.

mistakes.why: Temperature states take hacer, not ser.

culture.text: Spanish carries two second persons and a whole social grammar with them: tú for friends, family, students and anyone who has offered it; usted for strangers, officials, older people and most first meetings. Unlike German, the verb form makes the choice audible in every sentence (hablas / habla), so a learner who guesses is heard immediately — which is why A1 drills both from the first lesson.

reading.text: Ana llega nueva a la clase. Dice: «Hola, me llamo Ana. ¿Y tú?» Ben contesta: «Yo soy Ben. ¿De dónde eres?» — «De Sevilla. ¿Y tú?» — «De México.» Entra el profesor y dice: «Buenos días. Yo soy el señor García.» Todos dicen: «Buenos días, señor García.»
reading.gloss: Ana arrives new to the class. She says: 'Hello, my name is Ana. And you?' Ben answers: 'I am Ben. Where are you from?' — 'From Seville. And you?' — 'From Mexico.' The teacher comes in and says: 'Good morning. I am Mr García.' Everyone says: 'Good morning, Mr García.'

listening.script:
Ana: ¡Hola! Me llamo Ana. ¿Y tú?
Ben: Yo soy Ben. ¿Cómo estás?
Ana: Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?
Ben: Bien también. ¿De dónde eres?
listening.gloss: Ana: Hello! My name is Ana. And you? Ben: I am Ben. How are you? Ana: Fine, thanks. And you? Ben: Fine too. Where are you from?

mistakes.why: Feelings and states take estar; ser would describe a permanent quality.

mistakes.why: First meetings take usted; tú is offered, not assumed.

task.title: Introduce yourself twice
task.instructions: Write the same introduction twice in Spanish: once to a classmate (tú) and once to a professor's secretary at a first meeting (usted, surname). Read both aloud. Then change one word and check that the whole sentence still agrees — the verb ending, the possessive and the greeting all follow the person you chose, and a mixed pair is what a listener hears first.
